desc:
Two arrays a and b have the same length n. Pair every element of a with a different element of b, so that each element of b is used exactly once. The cost of a pair is the XOR of its two values, and the cost of a pairing is the sum of its pair costs.

Return the minimum possible total cost.

a = [1, 2], b = [2, 3] -> 2   (pair 1 with 3 and 2 with 2: cost 2 + 0)
a = [5], b = [9]       -> 12
hints: Try a recursion over the elements of a: element i is matched with some element of b that has not been used yet. What must the state remember?
The only thing that matters is which elements of b are already used. The number of used b elements tells you which element of a comes next, so a bitmask over b is a sufficient state.
Let dp[mask] be the minimum cost of matching the first popcount(mask) elements of a to the elements of b in mask. Extend each mask by one unused index of b.
editorial: Any pairing matches a[0] with some b-element, then a[1] with another, and so on. The cost of the remaining choices depends only on which b-elements are still free, so memoising over subsets of b removes the factorial blow-up of trying all permutations.

The DP has 2^n states, and each state tries at most n extensions, so the work is O(2^n * n), which is about 50,000 steps for n = 12. Every mask is reachable, since any subset of b can be matched with the first |mask| elements of a, and the answer is dp[full].
